solutions.text: The study controls temperature, lighting and noise and is double-blind, so the performance gap can reasonably be attributed to the ventilation difference, and the passage itself says the gap was widest on high-pollution days. The motivation claim is pure invention, keeping confounders equal does not show they never matter, and a wider gap on polluted days falls well short of proving that outdoor pollution directly impairs decision-making.

The passage states the fall in car journeys outright, but it merely reports the shopkeepers' lower revenues alongside it, so no causal link between the charge and the revenue dip is established. The purpose of the charge is never given (only how the revenue was spent), and the survey shows visitors still arrive, mostly by public transport. Reading the revenue fall as caused by the charge confuses a coincidence of facts with a demonstrated cause.

Givens: every student who passed attended all laboratory sessions; some students who attended all sessions won a scholarship; no scholarship winner was charged a fee.
Deduction 1: the second premise guarantees at least one student who both attended every session and won a scholarship.
Deduction 2: that student, being a scholarship winner, was not charged a fee.
Conclusion: at least one student who attended all of the laboratory sessions was not charged a fee, so that claim is forced.
Why the tempting claim fails: clearing the passers of fees would need some of them to have won scholarships, which no premise guarantees, and declaring every non-charged student an attendee merely reverses the first premise.

Givens: exactly one of Dana, Erik, Farid and Gus jammed the printer, and exactly one of the four statements is true.
Deduction 1: if Farid did it, the accusation of Erik is false, Erik's denial about Farid is false, Farid's own denial is false, and Gus's denial about Erik is true, giving exactly one truth.
Deduction 2: if Erik did it, the accusation of Erik, Erik's denial about Farid and Farid's denial are all true, three truths.
Deduction 3: if Dana or Gus did it, then Erik and Farid are both innocent, so the statements of Erik, Farid and Gus are all true, three truths again.
Conclusion: only Farid as the jammer leaves exactly one true statement, so Farid did it.
Why the tempting claim fails: accusing Erik would make Dana's statement true on top of the two denials, breaking the one-truth condition at once.

An equally large fall on roads with no cameras points to some town-wide cause (weather, traffic volumes, reporting habits) acting everywhere, which removes the council's grounds for crediting the cameras. Drivers feeling watched and thousands of recorded violations say nothing about what caused the accident drop, and an unchanged speed limit actually closes off an alternative explanation rather than weakening the case.

Givens: the rule is a one-way conditional: if the alarm sounds, all staff evacuate.
Deduction 1: a conditional of the form P implies Q is logically equivalent only to its contrapositive, not-Q implies not-P.
Deduction 2: here that contrapositive reads: if the staff do not evacuate, the fire alarm has not sounded.
Conclusion: the contrapositive is the only logically equivalent statement offered.
Why the tempting claims fail: evacuation implying the alarm sounded runs the arrow backwards, no alarm implying no evacuation only negates both parts without reversing them, the biconditional adds an unproven claim in the reverse direction, and a bare either-or is not a conditional at all.

Givens: Jana fixed in position 1; Gita somewhere left of Femi, Femi somewhere left of Ivo; Hugo immediately left of Kofi; the other five people fill positions 2 to 6.
Deduction 1: the Hugo-Kofi block must occupy positions 2-3, 3-4, 4-5 or 5-6, so there are four cases.
Deduction 2: block at 2-3 forces Gita, Femi, Ivo into positions 4, 5, 6 in that order.
Deduction 3: block at 3-4 forces Gita into 2 and Femi, Ivo into 5, 6.
Deduction 4: block at 4-5 forces Gita, Femi into 2, 3 and Ivo into 6.
Deduction 5: block at 5-6 forces Gita, Femi, Ivo into 2, 3, 4.
Conclusion: these four rows are the only valid arrangements, and Gita lands on position 2 or 4 in every one of them, so Gita in position 5 is impossible.
Why the tempting claims fail: Hugo on 2, Ivo on 4, Femi on 3 and Kofi on 5 each appear in one of the four rows, so none of them is ruled out.

Givens: lectures at 9:00, 11:00, 13:00 and 15:00; Chemistry earlier than Demography; Botany not at 9:00; Anthropology immediately before or after Botany.
Deduction 1: the Anthropology-Botany pair must occupy adjacent slots, 9:00-11:00, 11:00-13:00 or 13:00-15:00, giving five schedules to test.
Deduction 2: pair at 9:00-11:00 leaves Chemistry at 13:00 and Demography at 15:00.
Deduction 3: pair at 11:00-13:00, either internal order, leaves Chemistry at 9:00 and Demography at 15:00.
Deduction 4: pair at 13:00-15:00, either internal order, leaves Chemistry at 9:00 and Demography at 11:00.
Deduction 5: in all five valid schedules Demography comes after Chemistry, so Demography can never take the first slot.
Conclusion: Demography is not scheduled at 9:00, and this holds in every arrangement, so it must be true.
Why the tempting claims fail: Chemistry sits only at 9:00 or 13:00 (never at 11:00 or 15:00), Botany ranges over 11:00, 13:00 and 15:00, and Anthropology opens the day in only one of the five schedules.

Givens: five ranks with T fixed third; the chain S better than R better than Q; P, S, R and Q fill positions 1, 2, 4 and 5.
Deduction 1: Q needs both S and R ahead of it, and position 3 is taken, so Q can sit only fourth or fifth.
Deduction 2: with Q fifth, S and R take two of positions 1, 2 and 4 in that order and P takes the remainder, which gives three rankings.
Deduction 3: with Q fourth, S and R must take positions 1 and 2 and P is pushed to fifth, one ranking.
Deduction 4: in all four resulting rankings Q occupies fourth or fifth place.
Conclusion: Q is ranked either fourth or fifth, and this must be true.
Why the tempting claims fail: one ranking puts P first and S second, so S first, P second and S ahead of P each break, and R holds second place in three of the four rankings, so R fourth fails too.

The salt bridge is an ionic attraction between the positively charged lysine side chain and the negatively charged aspartate side chain. At pH 2 the aspartate side chain is protonated and neutral, so the attraction vanishes and that region of the tertiary structure is destabilised, while the covalent backbone and hence the amino acid sequence are untouched, since side-chain ionic bonds are not peptide bonds. No new bridge can form because aspartate does not turn positive, and uncharged groups do not attract more strongly than opposite charges.

Pepsin's optimum is near pH 2, so raising the stomach contents to roughly pH 7 leaves it working far below its maximum. The small intestine is unchanged, so trypsin, happiest near pH 8, keeps its normal activity there. Enzymes do not shift their optima to suit their surroundings, and trypsin in any case prefers alkaline conditions, so the claim that both enzymes need strongly acidic conditions is wrong.

Per glucose unit, glycolysis pays out 4 ATP (2 at phosphoglycerate kinase, 2 at pyruvate kinase). A free glucose molecule would also spend 1 ATP at hexokinase and 1 at phosphofructokinase, but a glycogen-derived unit enters already phosphorylated as glucose 6-phosphate, so only the phosphofructokinase ATP is spent: net = 4 - 1 = 3 ATP. Fermenting pyruvate to lactate merely regenerates NAD+ and changes no ATP figure.

The sodium-glucose cotransporter runs on the downhill sodium gradient, and that gradient exists only because the sodium-potassium pump spends ATP maintaining it (secondary active transport). Inactivate the pump and sodium leaks in until the gradient dissipates, so the cotransporter loses its driving force and glucose absorption by this route fails. The transporter's own lack of direct ATP use is irrelevant: its energy source is the pump.

The outside solution holds more non-penetrating solute than the cell sap, so it is hypertonic and water leaves the cell by osmosis. The protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the cell wall (plasmolysis), and the cell cannot burst because it is losing water while the rigid wall resists deformation rather than blocking osmosis. Every water-entry picture contradicts the direction of the concentration difference.

The nucleolus transcribes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosomal subunits. With that blocked, no new ribosomes reach the cytoplasm, so messenger RNA keeps being transcribed but is translated ever less efficiently and total protein synthesis falls. Secreted proteins are made on rough ER ribosomes drawing on the same subunit supply, the nucleolus has no protective role for mRNA, and DNA replication is untouched.

The substitution lies in the promoter, outside the coding sequence, so the mRNA sequence and therefore the amino acid sequence of the protein are unchanged. Because polymerase binds less well, transcription is less efficient and the protein is made in reduced amounts. Frameshifts need insertions or deletions rather than substitutions, a mutated promoter reduces transcription but does not destroy DNA, and this mutation plainly does affect the cell.

Step 1: in meiosis I nondisjunction both homologues of the pair go to the same pole, so after a normal meiosis II the four products are two with 24 chromosomes and two with 22; none is normal. Step 2: fertilisation by a normal sperm (23 chromosomes) gives 47 or 45 chromosomes depending on which product becomes the egg. The 24, 24, 23, 23 pattern with two normal products belongs to nondisjunction in meiosis II, and aneuploid eggs are certainly capable of being fertilised.

For each gene separately, Bb × Bb gives the recessive phenotype with probability 1/4. The genes assort independently, so P(bb and ll) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. The value 9/16 is instead the chance of showing both dominant traits.

Affected frequency q² = 1/2500, so q = 1/50 = 0.02 and p = 0.98. Carrier frequency = 2pq = 2 × 0.98 × 0.02 = 0.0392, which is roughly 0.04 = 1/25. The allele frequency itself is 1/50, and 1/2500 counts only affected individuals, so both undershoot the heterozygote total.

Chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope breaks down without needing the spindle, so treated cells reach a metaphase-like state with fully condensed chromosomes, each still two joined sister chromatids. With no microtubules nothing pulls the chromatids apart, anaphase never begins and the cells pile up there; colchicine blocks division rather than triggering it or sending cells back to interphase.

Step 1: with the proton return path blocked, the gradient builds until protons can no longer be pumped, so electron transport stalls even though oxygen is present. Step 2: NADH is no longer reoxidised and accumulates. Step 3: glycolysis needs NAD+ at its oxidation step, so the cell regenerates NAD+ by reducing pyruvate to lactate. The rival story, a dissipating gradient with accelerated transport, describes an uncoupler, which is the opposite of a blocked channel.

In the cross-bridge cycle, ATP binding to myosin is what detaches the head from actin. After death there is no ATP, so heads that have bound actin can never release: the cross-bridges lock and the muscle freezes in a contracted, rigid state. Filament lengths never change, the calcium has already leaked out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and tropomyosin's position depends on calcium, not ATP.

A narrowed outlet raises the resistance the left ventricle works against, so it must reach a higher pressure to eject, ejection is prolonged, and the wall thickens over time under the chronic load. Backflow from the aorta during diastole describes an incompetent (leaky) valve, not a narrowed one; the mitral valve is closed throughout systole; and the pulmonary circuit is not the first circuit to feel the problem.

Sub-atmospheric pleural pressure normally couples the lung's inward elastic recoil to the chest wall, keeping the lung expanded. When air leaks in and the pressure equals atmospheric, the recoil is unopposed, so the lung collapses inward while the chest wall springs outward. Nothing pushes air into the lung tissue and the alveolar elastic fibres are not destroyed; with no pressure difference there is simply nothing holding the lung open.

Carbon monoxide sits on the same haem sites as oxygen with vastly higher affinity, so most haemoglobin is locked up as carboxyhaemoglobin and the blood's oxygen content collapses. A pulse oximeter cannot optically distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so it reports a falsely reassuring high saturation. Dissolved plasma oxygen is a negligible share of transport, and the remaining sites hold oxygen more tightly, releasing less to tissues, so delivery falls rather than rises.

Glucose entering a blood capillary of the villus travels in the hepatic portal vein to the liver, crosses the liver sinusoids (a second capillary bed) and leaves by the hepatic vein, without passing the heart on the way. The lacteal carries fats in lymph rather than glucose, and the hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood to the liver instead of collecting absorbed nutrients.

The tablets raise circulating T4 above normal. Because feedback control is intact, the hypothalamus and pituitary respond to high T4 by cutting TRH and TSH secretion, so TSH is low while T4 is high. The patterns with high TSH get the feedback backwards, and oral thyroxine is absorbed (it is exactly how hypothyroidism is treated), so the blood levels are anything but normal.

Sweating without drinking makes the plasma more concentrated and reduces its volume, and both changes stimulate ADH release from the posterior pituitary. ADH makes the collecting ducts reabsorb water, so the urine becomes scant and concentrated, and hypothalamic osmoreceptors produce thirst. Falling ADH with copious dilute urine describes the response to drinking too much, the opposite scenario.

Falling blood glucose triggers the counter-regulatory hormones glucagon and adrenaline, which mobilise liver glycogen into glucose and produce the warning symptoms of hunger, trembling and sweating. In type 1 diabetes the pancreas cannot secrete extra insulin, storing glucose as glycogen would push the level the wrong way, and falling glucagon would deepen the hypoglycaemia.

Structure follows function: the oesophagus is scraped by swallowed food, so a many-layered squamous lining sacrifices absorption for abrasion resistance, while the intestine absorbs nutrients through a single thin layer that keeps diffusion distances short. The oesophagus digests nothing, and the single layer is a functional specialisation rather than a weakness.

Repair cells, oxygen and matrix building blocks reach a wound through blood vessels, and cartilage is essentially avascular, so supplies arrive only by slow diffusion through the matrix and healing drags on. Keratin is an epidermal protein, cartilage is connective tissue, and sitting beneath the skin does not physically block repair cells from reaching it.

The ten survivors hold 6 × 2 + 3 = 15 copies of allele A out of 20 alleles, a frequency of 15/20 = 0.75. A chance-driven crash to a handful of founders that shifts allele frequency is the bottleneck form of genetic drift. Counting only the homozygotes' alleles gives 12/20 = 0.60, and nothing in the story involves migration, selection or mutation.

Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol share a formula but differ in which carbon bears the OH group, so they are constitutional isomers. The R and S forms of butan-2-ol are non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers), and the cis and trans forms of pent-2-ene differ in the geometry about the double bond, so both of those pairs are stereoisomers. Cis and trans alkenes are diastereomers rather than mirror images, and a difference in position of a group never produces stereoisomers.

Given: 4.8 g of CH₄ (M = 16 g/mol), 4.8 g of O₂ (M = 32 g/mol), equation CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, molar volume 22.4 dm³/mol at STP.
Relationship: n = m ÷ M; the equation fixes a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio of methane to oxygen to carbon dioxide; gas volume = n × 22.4 dm³ at STP.
Substitute: n(CH₄) = 4.8 ÷ 16 = 0.30 mol; n(O₂) = 4.8 ÷ 32 = 0.15 mol.
Limiting check: 0.15 mol of O₂ burns only 0.15 ÷ 2 = 0.075 mol of CH₄, so the oxygen runs out first.
Hop: CO₂ formed = 0.075 mol (1:1 with the methane burned), so V = 0.075 × 22.4 = 1.68 dm³ at STP.
Hop: methane left = 0.30 - 0.075 = 0.225 mol, mass = 0.225 × 16 = 3.6 g.
Result: 1.68 dm³ of CO₂ forms at STP and 3.6 g of methane remains.
Classic slip: letting the 0.15 mol of oxygen stand for 0.15 mol of CO₂, which inflates the volume to 3.36 dm³ by ignoring the 2:1 oxygen requirement.

Given: 0.40 g of NaOH (M = 40 g/mol) made up to 1.0 dm³, then 10 cm³ of it diluted to 1.0 dm³; Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
Relationship: n = m ÷ M; NaOH is fully dissociated so [OH⁻] equals the NaOH concentration; pH + pOH = 14; dilution divides the concentration by the volume factor.
Substitute: n = 0.40 ÷ 40 = 0.010 mol, so the first solution has [OH⁻] = 0.010 ÷ 1.0 = 1.0 × 10⁻² mol/dm³.
Hop: pOH = 2, so pH = 14 - 2 = 12 in the first solution.
Dilution: factor = 1000 ÷ 10 = 100, so [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻² ÷ 100 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³.
Hop: pOH = 4.
Result: pH = 14 - 4 = 10.
Classic slip: reading the final pOH, 4, as the pH, or treating the hundredfold dilution as tenfold, which would give pH 11.

Given: Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ at the higher temperature; [OH⁻] = 0.010 mol/dm³ from fully dissociated NaOH.
Relationship: Kw = [H⁺] × [OH⁻], so [H⁺] = Kw ÷ [OH⁻], and pH = -log₁₀[H⁺].
Substitute: [H⁺] = (1.0 × 10⁻¹³) ÷ (1.0 × 10⁻²).
Hop: [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ mol/dm³.
Hop: pH = -log₁₀(1.0 × 10⁻¹¹) = 11.
Result: pH = 11 at this temperature.
Classic slip: dividing by the 25 °C value of Kw, 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, which lands on pH 12; the solution is still firmly alkaline even though neutral water here would read pH 6.5.

Given: 20 cm³ of 0.010 mol/dm³ HCl (strong, fully ionised) diluted to 400 cm³; log₁₀ 2 = 0.30.
Relationship: the dilution factor is V(final) ÷ V(initial); [H⁺] is divided by it, and each tenfold drop in [H⁺] raises pH by exactly 1, so ΔpH = log₁₀(dilution factor).
Substitute: dilution factor = 400 ÷ 20 = 20.
Hop: initial [H⁺] = 0.010 mol/dm³, so initial pH = 2.00.
Hop: ΔpH = log₁₀ 20 = log₁₀ 2 + log₁₀ 10 = 0.30 + 1.00 = 1.30.
Result: pH = 2.00 + 1.30 = 3.30 (check: [H⁺] = 0.010 ÷ 20 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³, and -log(5.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.30).
Classic slip: assuming a clean tenfold dilution, which gives pH 3.00, or a hundredfold one, which gives 4.00; the true factor of 20 needs the log of 2.

Boiling point tracks the strongest intermolecular force. Propane is non-polar (London forces only) and boils lowest; propanone adds a permanent dipole but has no O-H bond, so it cannot donate hydrogen bonds; ethanol hydrogen bonds in pairs; and ethanoic acid forms dimers held by two hydrogen bonds at once, needing the most energy to vaporise. The order is propane, then propanone, then ethanol, then ethanoic acid; the similar molar masses mean size cannot decide the ranking.

Given: rate proportional to [A]¹ and to [B]²; [A] doubled; [B] tripled.
Relationship: total rate factor = (change in A)^(order in A) × (change in B)^(order in B) = 2¹ × 3².
Hop: 3² = 9.
Hop: total = 2 × 9 = 18.
Result: the rate increases by a factor of 18.
Classic slip: dropping the square and computing 2 × 3 = 6, which treats the rate as first order in B.

Given: tetrathionate ion S₄O₆²⁻, four sulfur atoms treated as equivalent, oxygen = -2.
Relationship: oxidation numbers sum to the overall charge: 4x + 6 × (-2) = -2.
Substitute: 4x - 12 = -2.
Hop: 4x = -2 + 12 = 10.
Result: x = 10 ÷ 4 = +2.5, the average oxidation number per sulfur atom.
Classic slip: reporting +10, the total held by all four sulfur atoms together, as if it were one atom's average.

Given: sulfur in SO₃²⁻; nitrogen in N₂, NH₃, NO, NO₂ and N₂O; oxygen = -2; neutral molecules sum to 0.
Relationship: the sum of oxidation numbers equals the species' overall charge.
Hop 1: sulfur, x + 3 × (-2) = -2, so x = +4.
Hop 2: nitrogen in NO₂, x + 2 × (-2) = 0, so x = +4: a match.
Hop 3: sweep the rest: N₂ is 0 (element), NH₃ gives x + 3 = 0 so x = -3, NO gives x - 2 = 0 so x = +2, N₂O gives 2x - 2 = 0 so x = +1.
Result: only in NO₂ does nitrogen carry +4, the same as sulfur in the sulfite ion.
Classic slip: forgetting the -2 charge when computing sulfur, which gives +6 instead of +4 and sends the matching astray.

Given: first-order kinetics, half-life 20 minutes, elapsed time 60 minutes, initial amount 0.80 mol in a 2.0 dm³ vessel.
Relationship: each half-life halves the amount; number of half-lives = time ÷ half-life; concentration = amount ÷ volume.
Substitute: number of half-lives = 60 ÷ 20 = 3.
Hop 1: after 20 min, 0.80 ÷ 2 = 0.40 mol.
Hop 2: after 40 min, 0.40 ÷ 2 = 0.20 mol.
Hop 3: after 60 min, 0.20 ÷ 2 = 0.10 mol.
Hop 4: concentration = 0.10 ÷ 2.0 = 0.050 mol/dm³.
Result: 0.050 mol/dm³ after 60 minutes.
Classic slip: quoting the 0.10 as a concentration without dividing by the 2.0 dm³ vessel, or halving one time more, which would give 0.025 mol/dm³.

Given: X = 4.4 g of CO₂ (M = 12 + 32 = 44 g/mol); Y = 4.9 g of H₂SO₄ (M = 98 g/mol); Avogadro constant 6.02 × 10²³ per mol.
Relationship: n = m ÷ M; each CO₂ holds 2 oxygen atoms, each H₂SO₄ holds 4; atoms = n × atoms per molecule × 6.02 × 10²³.
Substitute X: n = 4.4 ÷ 44 = 0.10 mol of CO₂, giving 0.10 × 2 = 0.20 mol of oxygen atoms.
Substitute Y: n = 4.9 ÷ 98 = 0.050 mol of H₂SO₄, giving 0.050 × 4 = 0.20 mol of oxygen atoms.
Hop: 0.20 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.204 × 10²³ ≈ 1.2 × 10²³ atoms in each sample.
Result: both samples contain about 1.2 × 10²³ oxygen atoms.
Classic slip: doubling one conversion, for instance crediting each CO₂ with 4 oxygens, which yields 2.4 × 10²³ for one sample and breaks the equality.

Given: 50 cm³ of 0.20 mol/dm³ HCl; 150 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ NaOH; both fully ionised; Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴; log 2.5 = 0.40.
Relationship: n = c × V; H⁺ and OH⁻ neutralise 1:1; the surviving ion's concentration = leftover moles ÷ total volume; pH + pOH = 14.
Substitute: n(H⁺) = 0.050 × 0.20 = 0.010 mol; n(OH⁻) = 0.150 × 0.10 = 0.015 mol.
Hop: excess OH⁻ = 0.015 - 0.010 = 0.005 mol (the base wins).
Hop: total volume = 50 + 150 = 200 cm³ = 0.200 dm³, so [OH⁻] = 0.005 ÷ 0.200 = 0.025 mol/dm³.
Hop: pOH = -log(2.5 × 10⁻²) = 2 - 0.40 = 1.60.
Result: pH = 14 - 1.60 = 12.40.
Classic slip: skipping the division by the combined volume, which inflates [OH⁻] to 0.005 mol/dm³ and the pH to 13.00, or reporting the pOH of 1.60 as the pH.

Given: 1.08 g of Al (M = 27 g/mol); 100 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄; equation 2Al + 3H₂SO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3H₂; molar volume 22.4 dm³/mol at STP.
Relationship: n = m ÷ M or c × V; the reagent that runs out first fixes the yield; H₂ forms 1:1 with the acid consumed (3:3 in the equation).
Substitute: n(Al) = 1.08 ÷ 27 = 0.040 mol; n(H₂SO₄) = 0.100 × 0.10 = 0.010 mol.
Limiting check: consuming all the aluminium would need 0.040 × 3 ÷ 2 = 0.060 mol of acid, but only 0.010 mol exists, so the acid is limiting.
Hop: H₂ formed = 0.010 mol (1:1 with the acid).
Hop: V = 0.010 × 22.4 = 0.224 dm³ at STP.
Hop: aluminium consumed = 0.010 × 2 ÷ 3 ≈ 0.0067 mol ≈ 0.18 g, leaving about 1.08 - 0.18 = 0.90 g of aluminium unused.
Result: 0.224 dm³ of H₂ at STP, with aluminium in excess.
Classic slip: treating the 0.040 mol of aluminium as limiting, which multiplies the gas up to 1.344 dm³ and ignores the acid running dry.

Given: 500 cm³ of 0.20 mol/dm³ NaCl evaporated to exactly 200 cm³, no solute lost.
Relationship: n = c × V; evaporation removes solvent only, so n stays fixed and c(new) = n ÷ V(new).
Substitute: n = 0.500 dm³ × 0.20 mol/dm³ = 0.10 mol.
Hop: V(new) = 200 cm³ = 0.200 dm³.
Result: c(new) = 0.10 ÷ 0.200 = 0.50 mol/dm³.
Classic slip: multiplying by the volume ratio instead of dividing (0.20 × 200/500 = 0.08 mol/dm³), which reverses what removing water does.

Given: two solutions at pH 3.5 and pH 5.5 at 25 °C.
Relationship: pH = -log₁₀[H⁺], so each whole unit of pH is a factor of 10 in [H⁺], and the factor between two solutions is 10 raised to the pH difference.
Substitute: difference = 5.5 - 3.5 = 2.0 units.
Hop: factor = 10² = 100.
Result: the pH 3.5 solution has 100 times the hydrogen ion concentration of the pH 5.5 solution.
Classic slip: treating the pH scale as linear and multiplying the 2-unit gap by ten to get 20.

Given: log₁₀ 5 = 0.70; log₁₀ 3 = 0.48.
Relationship: 45 = 3² × 5, so log₁₀ 45 = 2 × log₁₀ 3 + log₁₀ 5 (product rule plus power rule).
Substitute: log₁₀ 45 = 2 × 0.48 + 0.70.
Hop: 2 × 0.48 = 0.96.
Result: 0.96 + 0.70 = 1.66.
Classic slip: reading 45 as 3 × 5² instead, which gives 0.48 + 2 × 0.70 = 1.88, or as 3 × 5, which gives 1.18.

Given: x² + kx + 9 = 0, asking for the values of k that give no real solutions.
Relationship: a quadratic has no real roots exactly when its discriminant k² - 4ac is negative.
Substitute: discriminant = k² - 4 × 1 × 9 = k² - 36.
Condition: k² - 36 < 0, that is k² < 36.
Hop: |k| < 6, so -6 < k < 6 with both ends excluded.
Result: no real solutions precisely when -6 < k < 6.
Classic slip: writing ≤ at both ends; at k = 6 or k = -6 the discriminant is zero and the equation has the repeated real root x = -3 or x = 3, which still counts as a real solution.

Given: sphere of radius 3 cm melted and recast as a cylinder of radius 2 cm; V(sphere) = (4/3)πr³; V(cylinder) = πr²h.
Relationship: melting conserves volume, so sphere volume = cylinder volume.
Substitute: V(sphere) = (4/3) × π × 3³ = (4/3) × 27 × π = 36π cm³.
Substitute: V(cylinder) = π × 2² × h = 4πh.
Equate: 4πh = 36π.
Result: h = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm.
Classic slip: dividing 36π by 2π instead of 4π, forgetting to square the cylinder's radius, which gives 18 cm.

Given: 3 red and 5 blue balls, 8 in all, two drawn without replacement.
Relationship: P(both red) and P(both blue) are mutually exclusive, so P(same colour) is their sum; each branch multiplies the first-draw and second-draw probabilities.
Substitute red: (3/8) × (2/7) = 6/56.
Substitute blue: (5/8) × (4/7) = 20/56.
Hop: sum = 6/56 + 20/56 = 26/56.
Result: 26/56 = 13/28.
Classic slip: computing the complement instead, the 30/56 chance of two different colours, and reporting 15/28.

Given: distance from start 0, 120, 300 and 540 m at times 0, 1, 2 and 3 minutes.
Relationship: average speed over one interval = distance gained ÷ time, with 1 minute = 60 s.
Hop 1: interval 1 covers 120 - 0 = 120 m, speed = 120 ÷ 60 = 2.0 m/s.
Hop 2: interval 2 covers 300 - 120 = 180 m, speed = 180 ÷ 60 = 3.0 m/s.
Hop 3: interval 3 covers 540 - 300 = 240 m, speed = 240 ÷ 60 = 4.0 m/s.
Compare: 4.0 m/s is the largest of the three.
Result: greatest one-minute average speed = 4.0 m/s.
Classic slip: dividing the whole 540 m by the total 180 s to get the overall 3.0 m/s, which blends the intervals instead of isolating the fastest one.

Given: √50 + √18 - √8, required in the form a√2.
Relationship: √(a² × b) = a√b, so extract the largest perfect square from each radicand.
Hop 1: √50 = √(25 × 2) = 5√2.
Hop 2: √18 = √(9 × 2) = 3√2.
Hop 3: √8 = √(4 × 2) = 2√2.
Combine: (5 + 3 - 2)√2 = 6√2.
Result: a = 6, value 6√2.
Classic slip: ignoring the minus sign and summing all coefficients to get 10, or flipping the sign of the middle term to get 4.

Given: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A and B) = 0.2.
Relationship: addition rule, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B); the subtraction removes the double-counted overlap.
Substitute: P(A or B) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 0.2.
Hop: 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9.
Result: 0.9 - 0.2 = 0.7.
Classic slip: stopping at 0.9 and never subtracting the 0.2 shared outcomes.

Given: velocity 14 m/s at 6.0 s; velocity 6 m/s at 8.0 s.
Relationship: a = Δv ÷ Δt; the magnitude keeps only the size of the answer.
Substitute: a = (6 - 14) ÷ (8.0 - 6.0).
Hop 1: Δv = 6 - 14 = -8 m/s.
Hop 2: Δt = 2.0 s, so a = -8 ÷ 2.0 = -4 m/s².
Result: magnitude of acceleration = 4 m/s² (the trolley is braking).
Classic slip: quoting the velocity change of 8 m/s as the acceleration without dividing by the 2.0 s interval.

Given: radius r = 50 m; speed v = 10 m/s; uniform circular motion.
Relationship: centripetal acceleration a = v² ÷ r, directed toward the centre at every instant.
Substitute: a = 10² ÷ 50.
Hop: 10² = 100, so a = 100 ÷ 50 = 2.0 m/s².
Result: acceleration of 2.0 m/s² pointing toward the centre of the bend.
Classic slip: dividing without squaring, 10 ÷ 50 = 0.20 m/s², or reasoning that constant speed means zero acceleration although the direction of travel keeps turning.

Given: 24 V battery of negligible internal resistance; 8.0 Ω in series with a parallel pair of 12 Ω and 6.0 Ω.
Relationship: parallel pair R = (R₁ × R₂) ÷ (R₁ + R₂); series resistances add; I = V ÷ R_total.
Substitute parallel: (12 × 6.0) ÷ (12 + 6.0) = 72 ÷ 18 = 4.0 Ω.
Hop: R_total = 8.0 + 4.0 = 12 Ω.
Substitute: I = 24 ÷ 12.
Result: I = 2.0 A.
Classic slip: dividing 24 V by the lone 8.0 Ω resistor to get 3.0 A, forgetting that the whole current must also cross the parallel section.

Given: m₁ = 0.40 kg of water at 20 °C; m₂ = 0.20 kg of water at 65 °C; insulated container; same specific heat capacity c.
Relationship: heat gained by the cold water = heat lost by the warm water, m₁c(T - 20) = m₂c(65 - T); c cancels.
Substitute: 0.40(T - 20) = 0.20(65 - T).
Expand: 0.40T - 8.0 = 13.0 - 0.20T.
Collect: 0.40T + 0.20T = 13.0 + 8.0, so 0.60T = 21.0.
Result: T = 21.0 ÷ 0.60 = 35 °C.
Classic slip: taking the plain midpoint (20 + 65) ÷ 2 = 42.5 °C, which weights both samples equally and ignores that the cold one has twice the mass.

Given: ρ = 800 kg/m³; depth h = 3.0 m; g = 10 m/s²; atmospheric pressure 100 kPa on the open surface.
Relationship: gauge pressure comes from the liquid column alone, p = ρgh; gauge means the atmosphere is excluded.
Substitute: p = 800 × 10 × 3.0.
Hop: 800 × 10 = 8000, so p = 8000 × 3.0 = 24000 Pa.
Result: p = 24 kPa gauge.
Classic slip: adding the 100 kPa of atmospheric pressure, which answers a different question (the absolute pressure, 124 kPa) instead of the gauge pressure asked.

Given: P = 2.0 kW; t = 3.0 minutes.
Relationship: E = P × t, with P in watts and t in seconds.
Convert: 2.0 kW = 2000 W; t = 3.0 × 60 = 180 s.
Substitute: E = 2000 × 180.
Hop: 2000 × 180 = 360000 J.
Result: E = 3.6 × 10⁵ J.
Classic slip: multiplying 2.0 by 3.0 with no unit conversion and stamping the 6.0 as × 10³ J, mixing kilowatts with minutes.
